questions.question: A tibble holds one numeric column `wage` for 200 workers. Which geom shows whether the wages have two peaks?
options: `geom_boxplot()`
`geom_point()`
`geom_histogram()`
`geom_line()`

questions.question: Two numeric columns are plotted against each other with ggplot2. When is `geom_line()` the right geom rather than `geom_point()`?
options: When x is time, so that the order of the observations carries meaning.
Whenever both columns are numeric, as lines are clearer than single points.
When x is a categorical column, such as the name of a country.
When there are so many rows that single points can no longer be read.

questions.question: In a box plot drawn with `geom_boxplot()`, what does the line inside the box mark?
options: The mean of the values in the group.
The midpoint between the first and third quartile.
The value that occurs most often in the group.
The median of the values in the group.

questions.question: A line plot is stored as `p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = Year, y = v)) + geom_line()`. What does `p + geom_point()` show?
options: Only the points: the second geom replaces the line drawn by `geom_line()`.
The same line with a point on top of it at every row of `d`.
The line and the points in two separate panels placed side by side.
An error, because a plot made with `ggplot()` can hold only one geom.

questions.question: A tibble `d` has a character column `sector` with three sectors and a numeric column `wage`. Which call compares the quartiles and medians of `wage` across the sectors?
options: `ggplot(d, aes(x = sector, y = wage)) + geom_boxplot()`
`ggplot(d, aes(x = wage)) + geom_histogram()`
`ggplot(d, aes(x = sector, y = wage)) + geom_line()`
`ggplot(d, aes(x = sector, y = wage)) + geom_point()`

questions.question: A tibble `d` has the numeric columns `size` and `price` for 50 flats. Which call shows how `price` is related to `size`?
options: `ggplot(d, aes(x = size)) + geom_histogram()`
`ggplot(d, aes(x = size, y = price)) + geom_line()`
`ggplot(d, aes(x = size, y = price)) + geom_point()`
`ggplot(d, aes(x = size, y = price)) + geom_boxplot()`

questions.question: A tibble `d` has the columns `Country` (two countries), `Year` (2019 to 2021 for each) and numeric `v`. Which call draws one line per country?
options: `ggplot(d, aes(x = Year, y = v)) + geom_line(color = "Country")`
`ggplot(d, aes(x = Year, y = v)) + geom_line(group = Country)`
`ggplot(d, aes(x = Country, y = v, color = Year)) + geom_line()`
`ggplot(d, aes(x = Year, y = v, color = Country)) + geom_line()`

questions.question: A tibble `d` has a numeric column `wage` with 40 values. What happens when R runs `ggplot(d, aes(x = wage)) + geom_histogram()`?
options: R stops with an error, because `binwidth` or `bins` has to be given.
It is drawn with 30 bins, and a message suggests a better `binwidth`.
It is drawn with one bar for each distinct value of `wage`.
It is drawn with bins of width 1, the default `binwidth`.

questions.question: A tibble `d` has the numeric columns `wage` and `hours`. What happens when R draws `ggplot(d, aes(x = wage, y = hours)) + geom_histogram()`?
options: An error: `geom_histogram()` counts one variable and must not get both x and y.
A histogram of `wage` whose bar heights are the total `hours` in each bin.
A histogram of `hours`, because the y mapping takes priority over x.
A scatter plot of `hours` against `wage`, drawn with thin bars instead of points.

questions.question: The numeric vector `x <- c(3, 7, 8, 12, 15)` is not stored in a data frame. Which single call draws a histogram of `x`?
options: `plot(x)`
`geom_histogram(x)`
`hist(x)`
`ggplot(x) + geom_histogram()`

questions.question: A tibble holds `v` for two countries in the years 2019 to 2021, one row per country and year, with a column `Country`. What does `ggplot(d, aes(x = Year, y = v)) + geom_line()` draw?
options: Two separate lines, one per country, both in the same default colour.
Two lines in different colours, with a legend for `Country`.
One line through the rows in stored order: first one country, then the other.
One line that jumps up and down between the two countries at every year.

questions.question: A student plots 12 exam scores between 40 and 95 with `geom_histogram()` and no other argument. Most bars have height 0 or 1. What is the best reading of this plot?
options: The scores have many gaps, so the distribution truly has several peaks.
The 30 default bins are too many for 12 values; try a wider `binwidth`.
The heights are densities, which stay small whenever there are few values.
The data contain missing values, which ggplot2 draws as empty bins.

questions.question: What bars does `ggplot(tibble(x = c(2, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13)), aes(x = x)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0)` draw, from left to right?
options: Three bars, of heights 2, 3 and 1.
Three bars, of heights 1, 3 and 2.
Three bars, of heights 2, 2 and 2.
Six bars, each of height 1.

questions.question: A box plot is drawn for the values 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 30, whose first and third quartiles are 12.5 and 15.5. At which value does the upper whisker end?
options: At 20
At 16
At 30

questions.question: A tibble `d` has a character column `g` with two groups of five values and a numeric column `y`. Which call draws box plots with every observation shown as a point on top of the boxes?
options: `ggplot(d, aes(x = g, y = y)) + geom_point() + geom_boxplot()`
`ggplot(d, aes(x = g, y = y)) + geom_boxplot(geom_point())`
`ggplot(d, aes(x = g, y = y)) + geom_boxplot(points = TRUE)`
`ggplot(d, aes(x = g, y = y)) + geom_boxplot() + geom_point()`

questions.question: For `d <- tibble(level = c("mid", "mid", "low", "low", "high", "high"), y = c(5, 6, 1, 2, 3, 4))`, in which order from left to right does `ggplot(d, aes(x = level, y = y)) + geom_boxplot()` draw the boxes?
options: mid, low, high
high, low, mid
low, mid, high
low, high, mid

questions.question: Group A has 6 observations and group B has 600, and their quartiles, medians and whisker ends are the same, with no outliers. How do their boxes from `geom_boxplot()` differ?
options: They look the same: a box plot does not show how many observations a group has.
Box B is wider, because the default box width grows with the group size.
Box A shows its six values as points, as small groups are drawn point by point.
Box A has shorter whiskers, because fewer values give a smaller spread.

questions.question: For a continuous variable $X$, a box plot of a large sample draws the upper edge of the box at the sample's third quartile. Which property of the distribution of $X$ does this edge estimate?
options: The value $q$ with $\mathbb{P}(X\ge q)=0.75$, above which three quarters of the values lie.
The mean plus one standard deviation, $\mathbb{E}[X]+\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}$.
The largest value that is not an outlier, at most 1.5 box lengths above the box.
The value $q$ with $\mathbb{P}(X\le q)=0.75$, below which three quarters of the values lie.

questions.question: For `d <- tibble(year = rep(c(2019, 2020), each = 4), wage = c(10, 12, 14, 16, 20, 22, 24, 26))`, what does `ggplot(d, aes(x = year, y = wage)) + geom_boxplot()` draw?
options: Two boxes, one for 2019 and one for 2020, as for a character column.
An error, because `geom_boxplot()` accepts only a character column as x.
One box for all eight wages, with a warning about a continuous x aesthetic.
Two boxes, with a warning that `year` should first be turned into a factor.

questions.question: With ggplot2 loaded, what does `p <- ggplot(tibble(x = c(1, 2, 2, 3, NA, 4, 5, 5)), aes(x = x)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1); sum(layer_data(p)[["count"]])` return?
